products.title: WonderCave Enterprise Security Suite & Vulnerability Scanners
products.subtitle: Commercial-grade automated application auditing, crawler engines, and continuous attack surface monitoring.
products.content:
## Enterprise Product Portfolio Overview

The WonderCave Enterprise Security Suite delivers high-velocity, automated vulnerability detection and continuous perimeter surveillance for modern software engineering teams. Engineered from the ground up to support modern distributed microservices, single-page web applications (SPAs), GraphQL APIs, and cloud-native containers, our scanners combine deep protocol crawling with mathematically verified exploit payloads to eliminate false positives.

![High Tech Server Racks](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1558494949-ef010cbdcc31?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 1: Scalable automated crawler workers running across distributed Kubernetes nodes.*

---

## Real-World Enterprise Deployment Story: Global Fintech CI/CD Integration

"Prior to deploying WonderCave Enterprise Scanner, our security team spent 15 hours every week manually vetting false alarms generated by legacy SAST/DAST tools," explains David Keller, VP of Infrastructure Security. "By integrating the WonderCave headless crawler directly into our GitLab CI pipeline, automated scans execute against ephemeral preview environments on every pull request. Flaws such as BOLA, missing CSRF tokens, and reflected DOM sinks are caught and blocked before reaching staging, reducing our mean-time-to-remediate (MTTR) by 72%."

---

## Core Product Offerings

### 1. WonderCave Headless Dynamic Vulnerability Scanner
* **Deep Single-Page Application (SPA) Crawling**: Executes full Chrome headless browser engines to crawl dynamic React, Vue, Angular, and Next.js applications.
* **Active Payload Verification**: Validates exploitability in a sandbox before alerting developers, reducing false positives to virtually zero.
* **API Specification Ingestion**: Natively ingests OpenAPI/Swagger, Postman collections, and GraphQL introspection schemas to fuzz undocumented endpoints.

### 2. Attack Surface Management (ASM) & Continuous Perimeter Surveillance
* **Autonomous Asset Discovery**: Continuously monitors internet-facing subdomains, SSL/TLS certificates, cloud buckets (AWS S3, GCP Buckets), and DNS records.
* **Zero-Day Exposure Alerts**: Automatically matches newly published CVEs against your organization's fingerprinted software versions.

### 3. Developer Remediation Engine & IDE Plugins
* **Instant Pull Request Comments**: Generates automated code fixes and parameterized queries directly on GitHub and GitLab pull requests.
* **Interactive Sandbox Replay**: Generates one-click sandbox links where developers can replay the exact HTTP request sequence that triggered the vulnerability.

![Code Screen Inspector](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1555066931-4365d14bab8c?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 2: Real-time vulnerability diagnosis and interactive payload debugging.*

---

## Automated CI/CD Pipeline Configuration Example

```yaml
# .github/workflows/wondercave-security-audit.yml
name: WonderCave Security Pipeline
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  security-audit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: WonderCave Automated Scanner Action
        uses: wondercave/scanner-action@v2
        with:
          target-url: https://staging.internal.net
          api-spec: ./docs/openapi.json
          fail-on-severity: HIGH
          auth-token: ${{ secrets.WONDERCAVE_SCANNER_KEY }}
```

---

## Enterprise Support & Cloudflare Worker Compatibility

All WonderCave tooling is built to operate seamlessly with modern serverless architectures, including Cloudflare Workers, Cloudflare Pages, AWS Lambda, and on-premises air-gapped data centers under the leadership of Nayem Hasan at `wondercave.nayem.net`.

solutions.content:
## Industry Security Architectures

Modern organizations operate under rigorous regulatory scrutiny and relentless threat actor targeting. A generic, one-size-fits-all security strategy inevitably fails when applied to specialized operational environments—such as healthcare PACS imaging networks, high-frequency banking ledgers, or industrial supervisory control (SCADA) systems. WonderCave designs tailored defensive architectures aligned with industry-specific threat models.

![Industrial Manufacturing Operations](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1581091226825-a6a2a5aee158?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 1: Converged Operational Technology (OT) and Information Technology (IT) perimeters.*

---

## Sector-Specific Solution Matrix

### 1. Financial Services & FinTech (PCI-DSS 4.0 & SOC 2 Type II)
* **Threat Profile**: Credential stuffing, payment gateway manipulation, account takeover (ATO), and fraudulent wire execution.
* **Architecture Solution**: Continuous API authorization enforcement, zero-trust microsegmentation, and hardware-backed cryptographic signing for transaction mutations.

### 2. Healthcare & Life Sciences (HIPAA & HITECH Compliance)
* **Threat Profile**: Targeted ransomware attacks, electronic health record (EHR) database theft, and medical IoT device tampering.
* **Architecture Solution**: Attribute-based access control (ABAC), automated data-at-rest field-level encryption, and network perimeter isolation for legacy diagnostic appliances.

### 3. Industrial Manufacturing & Energy (IEC 62443 & NIST SP 800-82)
* **Threat Profile**: Air-gap bridging, supply chain firmware tampering, and operational downtime via ICS/SCADA protocol sabotage.
* **Architecture Solution**: Unidirectional security gateways, protocol fuzzing for Modbus/DNP3, and automated anomaly detection on sensor telemetry.

### 4. Retail & E-Commerce Platforms (Magecart & Bot Mitigation)
* **Threat Profile**: Digital credit card skimming, inventory hoarding bots, and web cache deception on user cart checkouts.
* **Architecture Solution**: Strict Content Security Policy (CSP Level 3), Subresource Integrity (SRI) hashing on third-party scripts, and Cloudflare edge rate-limiting.

![Network Architecture Diagram](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1451187580459-43490279c0fa?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 2: Zero-trust microsegmentation topology across distributed multi-cloud nodes.*

---

## Point-Based Implementation Roadmap

1. **Phase 1: Automated Asset Discovery & Threat Modeling**: Map all external endpoints, third-party connectors, and data ingress points.
2. **Phase 2: Gap Analysis against Regulatory Mandates**: Benchmark existing controls against NIST CSF, ISO 27001, and sector standards.
3. **Phase 3: Remediation & Automated CI/CD Integration**: Deploy automated scanning and zero-trust policies across development pipelines.
4. **Phase 4: Continuous Red-Team Verification**: Validate defensive efficacy through simulated adversary emulation exercises.

## Research Library & Technical Knowledge Base

The WonderCave Resources library is a peer-reviewed repository of technical whitepapers, protocol analysis teardowns, and defensive engineering guides. Authored by active security researchers and penetration testers, our research provides rigorous, reproducible methodologies for diagnosing and eliminating vulnerabilities in production web infrastructure.

![Technical Library and Research Data](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1516321318423-f06f85e504b3?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 1: Deep technical literature and empirical vulnerability research records.*

---

## Featured Research Papers & Whitepapers

* **Automating Zero-Trust Authorization in Microservice Meshes**: A 45-page empirical study on attribute-based access control (ABAC) overhead and security guarantees in Istio and Envoy proxy networks.
* **The Evolution of Modern Web Cache Attacks**: Systematic analysis of 12 major CDN providers evaluating path delimiter normalization, unkeyed header reflections, and edge cache poisoning.
* **Securing Autonomous Generative Agents in Enterprise Cloud**: Formal models for preventing indirect prompt injection and unconstrained tool invocation in production LLM workflows.

---

## Recommended Defensive Architecture Books & Standards

1. *The Web Application Hacker's Handbook (2nd Edition)* by Dafydd Stuttard & Marcus Pinto
2. *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann (Security & Fault Tolerance Chapters)
3. *Zero Trust Networks* by Gilman & Barth
4. *NIST Special Publication 800-53 (Rev. 5)*: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems

![Security Engineer at Work](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1550751827-4bd374c3f58b?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 2: Empirical analysis of network anomalies and protocol state machines.*

---

## Point-Based Self-Study Guide for Security Engineers

* **Step 1: Protocol Mastery**: Study RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), and RFC 7519 (JSON Web Tokens).
* **Step 2: Threat Modeling**: Practice stride threat modeling on simple distributed architectures (Auth, API, DB).
* **Step 3: Laboratory Exploitation**: Complete the WonderCave interactive exploit challenges.
* **Step 4: Defensive Remediation**: Implement secure cryptographic token verification in your favorite language.

learning-paths.content:
## Educational Methodology & Curriculum Overview

WonderCave provides structured, zero-cost, commercial-grade cybersecurity training tailored for modern technological challenges. Our curriculums bridge theoretical vulnerability mechanics with practical, hands-on exploitation and defensive engineering. Each track consists of interactive sandbox environments, step-by-step video walkthroughs, and verified proof-of-concept exercises.

![Student and Technology Learning](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1523050854058-8df90110c9f1?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 1: Structured modular learning and interactive skill verification in cybersecurity.*

---

## Real-World Practitioner Story: Transitioning from Development to Offensive Security

"When I started as a junior frontend developer, security was merely an afterthought—something a security team evaluated two days before a major release," shares Maya Lin, now a Senior Application Security Engineer at a Fortune 500 fintech firm. "Through structured hands-on learning, understanding how an attacker perceives DOM sinks, ambient credentials, and cache boundaries completely altered the way I write code. Within 12 months of mastering these interactive modules, I was able to identify three zero-day vulnerabilities in our core payment gateway."

---

## Core Certification Paths

### 1. Web Application Penetration Tester (WAPT Track)
* **Prerequisites**: Basic understanding of HTTP/HTTPS, browser dev tools, and JavaScript.
* **Module 1**: Reconnaissance, network scanning, and sub-domain enumeration using Nmap and Amass.
* **Module 2**: In-depth exploitation of the OWASP Top 10 (SQLi, XSS, CSRF, XXE, SSRF, IDOR).
* **Module 3**: Authentication bypasses, OAuth 2.0 implementation flaws, and JWT key confusion attacks.
* **Capstone Exercise**: Black-box penetration test against a simulated multi-tier banking application.

### 2. Cloud Security & Infrastructure Hardening (CSI Track)
* **Prerequisites**: Linux command line proficiency, Docker fundamentals, and cloud concepts.
* **Module 1**: AWS and GCP IAM least privilege governance, service accounts, and role assumption.
* **Module 2**: Container security, Kubernetes pod security standards, and CI/CD supply-chain hardening.
* **Module 3**: Microservice network policies, zero-trust service meshes (Istio/Linkerd), and egress filtering.

### 3. AI & LLM Security Engineering (ALSE Track)
* **Prerequisites**: Python proficiency and basic understanding of Transformer architectures.
* **Module 1**: Direct and indirect prompt injection attacks, jailbreak engineering, and defense benchmarks.
* **Module 2**: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector poisoning and data exfiltration.
* **Module 3**: Tool-calling authorization controls, sandboxed agent execution, and human-in-the-loop policies.

![Team Collaboration Lab](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1517430816045-df4b7de11d1d?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 2: Real-time telemetry and peer collaboration inside WonderCave sandboxes.*

---

## Point-Based Learning Milestones

* **Phase 1: Diagnostic Fundamentals**: Complete interactive quizzes on network protocols, TCP handshakes, and cryptographic hashing.
* **Phase 2: Laboratory Mastery**: Solve 25+ standalone exploit challenges in isolated browser sandboxes.
* **Phase 3: Code Remediation**: Submit pull requests fixing vulnerable application repositories to verify defensive coding skills.
* **Phase 4: Official Assessment**: Undertake a timed 24-hour practical exam evaluated by our senior security researchers.

---

## Academic References & Industry Alignment

* **NICE Cybersecurity Workforce Framework**: Work Roles SP-DEV-001 (Secure Software Assessor) & PR-CDA-001 (Cyber Defense Analyst)
* **OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG v4.2)**

latest-topics.title: Latest Topics
latest-topics.subtitle: Social Engineering & Wireless Attacks
latest-topics.content:
## Social Engineering

Social engineering, in the context of information security, refers to psychological manipulation of people into performing actions or divulging confidential information.

*   **Phishing**: An e-mail fraud method in which the perpetrator sends out legitimate-looking email in an attempt to gather personal and financial information from recipients.
*   **Baiting**: Like the real-world Trojan Horse that uses physical media and relies on the curiosity or greed of the victim.
*   **Tailgating**: An attacker, seeking entry to a restricted area secured by unattended, electronic access control, simply walks in behind a person who has legitimate access.

## Wireless Network Attacks

*   **Unintentional association**: When one wireless network overlaps with another, allowing a user to unintentionally jump from one into the other.
*   **MAC spoofing**: Theft of the identity of a computer that has network privileges.

learning-materials.subtitle: Understanding Malware and Common Attacks
learning-materials.content:
## Malware : A Hackers Henchman

Malware is defined by its malicious intent, acting against the requirements of the computer user. 

### Types of Malware

*   **Adware**: Automatically delivers advertisements. Often bundled with spyware.
*   **Spyware**: Functions by spying on user activity without their knowledge. Includes activity monitoring, collecting keystrokes, data harvesting.
*   **Bot**: Software programs created to automatically perform specific operations. Often used in botnets for DDoS attacks.
*   **Ransomware**: Holds a computer system captive while demanding a ransom.
*   **Trojan Horse**: Disguises itself as a normal file or program to trick users into downloading and installing malware.
*   **Worm**: Spread over computer networks by exploiting operating system vulnerabilities.

academy.title: WonderCave: Complete Guide to Ethical Hacking & Defensive Systems
academy.subtitle: Demystifying cybersecurity through rigorous hands-on laboratory exercises and responsible disclosure ethics.
academy.content:
## Mission Statement & Educational Philosophy

Cybercrime inflicts over $8 trillion in global damages annually, threatening critical infrastructure, healthcare institutions, and digital privacy. WonderCave was founded on a singular premise: to safeguard society's digital foundations, defenders must comprehend the precise mindset, methodologies, and technical toolsets employed by elite adversaries. 

All content produced at WonderCave is provided free of charge for ethical educational and defensive research purposes, under the supervision of lead security researcher Nayem Hasan at `wondercave.nayem.net`.

![Cyber Security Operations](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1550751827-4bd374c3f58b?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 1: Security Operations Center (SOC) monitoring and proactive threat intelligence.*

---

## Real-World Ethical Disclosure Case Study: Securing Open Source Infrastructure

In 2021, an independent security researcher affiliated with WonderCave identified an unauthenticated Remote Code Execution flaw in an enterprise document indexing daemon used by thousands of universities. Rather than selling the zero-day on underground exploit broker forums, the researcher followed our responsible disclosure framework:
1. Privately notified the maintainers with a complete proof-of-concept and detailed remediation patch.
2. Coordinated with MITRE to assign a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifier.
3. Provided a 90-day grace period for downstream package managers to distribute signed patches before publishing educational teardowns.

This responsible action shielded an estimated 4 million student records from unauthorized compromise.

---

## The Hacker's Hierarchy & Ethical Categorization

* **White Hat Hackers (Ethical Security Researchers)**: Professionals who discover security weaknesses with explicit authorization. They adhere strictly to the principle of "do no harm" and collaborate with organizations to fortify systems.
* **Gray Hat Hackers**: Individuals who probe systems without prior authorization, but without malicious or extortionist intent. They typically disclose findings publicly or seek bug bounty rewards.
* **Black Hat Hackers (Malicious Cybercriminals)**: Actors motivated by financial gain, corporate espionage, geopolitical sabotage, or notoriety who weaponize zero-days against unsuspecting targets.

---

## Essential Technical Tooling Practiced in the Academy

### 1. Network Discovery & Packet Analysis
* **Nmap**: Active host discovery, port scanning, OS fingerprinting, and automated NSE vulnerability scripting.
* **Wireshark & Tshark**: Deep packet inspection, TLS handshake debugging, and protocol anomaly detection.

### 2. Web Application Assessment & Interception Proxies
* **Burp Suite & OWASP ZAP**: HTTP traffic interception, parameter fuzzing, repeater payload testing, and WebSocket auditing.
* **SQLmap & ParamSpider**: Automated SQL injection detection and hidden URL query discovery.

### 3. Exploitation & Post-Exploitation Frameworks
* **Metasploit Framework**: Modular attack payloads, auxiliary scanners, and meterpreter shell environments.
* **Ghidra & Radare2**: Binary disassembly, reverse engineering, and decompiler analysis.

![Terminal Matrix View](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1518770660439-4636190af475?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 2: Hands-on console telemetry inside the WonderCave ethical hacking curriculum.*

---

## Core Pillars of Responsible Disclosure

1. **Explicit Authorization**: Never test, scan, or probe any IP address, domain, or API without verified written authorization from the system owner.
2. **Harm Minimization**: Refrain from executing Denial-of-Service attacks, corrupting production databases, or accessing private personal data beyond demonstrating proof of concept.
3. **Encrypted Communication**: Always communicate vulnerability details via PGP-encrypted email channels or official security disclosure portals.
4. **Coordinated Release**: Honor agreed-upon vendor remediation timelines to allow proper patch deployment prior to public disclosure.

---

## Academic References & Global Legal Standards

* **Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)**: 18 U.S. Code § 1030 Legal Scope
* **UK Computer Misuse Act 1990**: Section 1 Unauthorized Access Provisions
* **ISO/IEC 29147:2018**: Information Technology – Vulnerability Disclosure
* **ISO/IEC 30111:2019**: Information Technology – Vulnerability Handling Processes

services.subtitle: Professional IT security evaluation
services.content:
## What is Penetration Testing?

Penetration testing evaluates an organization's ability to protect its networks, applications, endpoints and users from external or internal attempts to circumvent its security controls.

### Pen Test Strategies

1.  **Targeted testing**: Performed by the organization's IT team and the penetration testing team working together.
2.  **External testing**: Targets a company's externally visible servers or devices including domain name servers (DNS), e-mail servers, Web servers or firewalls.
3.  **Internal testing**: Mimics an inside attack behind the firewall by an authorized user with standard access privileges.
4.  **Blind testing**: Simulates the actions and procedures of a real attacker by severely limiting the information given to the person or team that's performing the test beforehand.

## Target Mapping

Finding the perfect target for your attack is not as simple as it sounds. You have to be strategic in the way you conduct your research. The objective of mapping your target is to determine what and who you are attacking before penetrating the system.

### Scanning the Target Network

You can begin to use scanning software to find and record any hosts that are accessible online. Tools like Nmap, SuperScan, and NetScan Tools Pro are able to ping the hostname of the domain or multiple IP addresses simultaneously.

### Exposing System Vulnerabilities

Assuming you find some vulnerability in your target's system, you can then start checking if these security gaps are exploitable. The automated method involves the use of tools such as QualysGuard or Nexpose.

sql-injection.title: SQL Injection (SQLi) Vulnerabilities & Deep Exploitation
sql-injection.subtitle: Bypassing database query logic, extracting sensitive relational records, and achieving remote command execution.
sql-injection.content:
## Executive Threat Profile: SQL Injection (CWE-89)

SQL Injection (SQLi) remains one of the most destructive and prevalent web application vulnerabilities in modern software engineering. It occurs when untrusted user input is directly concatenated or interpolated into a dynamic database query string, allowing an attacker to manipulate the query structure, bypass authentication, exfiltrate confidential database rows, tamper with existing records, and potentially execute administrative operating system commands through database stored procedures.

![Database Query Architecture](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1544383835-bda2bc66a55d?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 1: Relational database architecture and untrusted query boundary analysis.*

---

## Real-World Breach Case Study: The Sony Pictures Security Compromise

In a benchmark cybersecurity incident, attackers leveraged a straightforward Blind SQL Injection flaw in Sony Pictures' public web portal. By injecting malicious SQL logic into unvalidated search parameters, the attackers bypassed front-end authentication layers and extracted cleartext passwords, administrator hashes, email databases, and proprietary corporate communications of over one million accounts. 

The post-incident analysis revealed that the application was constructing SQL statements using simple string interpolation:
`SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id = ' + userInput + '`
This allowed attackers to append `UNION SELECT` operators and dump the entire database schema without triggering perimeter alarms.

---

## Anatomy of the Vulnerability: Code Comparison

### 1. Vulnerable Implementation (Dynamic String Concatenation)
```sql
-- Insecure PHP / Node.js query construction
SELECT id, username, password_hash, email, role 
FROM accounts 
WHERE email = 'admin@wondercave.com' AND password = '' OR '1'='1' --';
```

When the user enters `' OR '1'='1' --` in the password field, the boolean expression evaluates to true for the first matching row, immediately authenticating the attacker as the primary administrative account.

### 2. Hardened Remediation (Parameterized Prepared Statements)
```typescript
// Secure TypeScript / Node.js implementation with TypeORM / pg parameterized query
import { Pool } from 'pg';

const pool = new Pool();

export async function authenticateUser(email: string, passwordHash: string) {
  const query = `
    SELECT id, username, email, role 
    FROM accounts 
    WHERE email = $1 AND password_hash = $2
    LIMIT 1;
  `;
  // Values are safely passed to the database engine separately from AST parsing
  const { rows } = await pool.query(query, [email, passwordHash]);
  return rows[0] || null;
}
```

![Network Packet Inspection](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1558494949-ef010cbdcc31?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 2: Intercepting and analyzing raw SQL payload exchanges in sandbox lab traffic.*

---

## Point-Based Exploitation Vector Breakdown

* **In-Band SQLi (Classic & UNION-Based)**: The attacker exploits the same channel of communication to launch the attack and harvest results. Results are echoed directly onto the returned web page.
  * *Payload*: `' UNION SELECT null, username, password FROM users --`
* **Inferential SQLi (Blind & Boolean-Based)**: The web application does not echo database output. The attacker sends payloads that force the application to return different HTTP response codes or content based on a true/false condition.
  * *Payload*: `' AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(password,1,1) FROM users WHERE username='admin')='a' --`
* **Time-Based Blind SQLi**: Injects database sleep commands (e.g., `pg_sleep(10)` or `WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:10'`) to infer character values through delayed HTTP server responses.
* **Out-of-Band (OOB) SQLi**: Forces the database server to perform DNS or HTTP lookups to an attacker-controlled listener (e.g., Burp Collaborator) via `UTL_HTTP` in Oracle or `xp_dirtree` in Microsoft SQL Server.

---

## Defense-in-Depth Mitigation Checklist

1. **Mandatory Parameterized Queries**: Enforce parameterized prepared statements across all Object-Relational Mappers (ORMs) and native drivers.
2. **Principle of Least Privilege**: The database connection string must operate under a restricted role without `DROP`, `ALTER`, or `xp_cmdshell` privileges.
3. **Strict Input Allow-Listing**: Validate incoming identifiers (such as column ordering or table names) against an immutable enum allow-list.
4. **WAF Layer Signatures**: Deploy Web Application Firewall rules to block canonical SQL syntax tokens in URL query strings.

---

## Formal Standards & Academic References

* **OWASP Top 10**: [A03:2021 – Injection](https://owasp.org/Top10/A03_2021-Injection/)
* **Common Weakness Enumeration**: [CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html)
* **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5**: Control SI-10 (Information Input Validation) and AC-6 (Least Privilege)
* **MITRE ATT&CK**: Technique T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application)

cross-site-scripting.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — DOM, Reflected & Stored Exploitation
cross-site-scripting.subtitle: Weaponizing browser execution environments, stealing session cookies, and establishing persistent client-side C2.
cross-site-scripting.content: ## Executive Threat Profile: Cross-Site Scripting (CWE-79) Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is a client-side code injection vulnerability that occurs when a web application accepts untrusted data and renders it in the victim's web browser without contextual sanitization, escaping, or Content Security Policy (CSP) enforcement. Once arbitrary JavaScript executes within the victim's origin context, the adversary gains full access to session tokens, local storage, DOM nodes, web camera APIs, and can perform state-changing HTTP requests on the victim's behalf. ![Frontend Code and DOM Tree](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1555066931-4365d14bab8c?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000) *Figure 1: DOM tree manipulation and script execution context inside modern browser engines.* --- ## Real-World Breach Case Study: The British Airways Magecart Digital Skimming In 2018, the Magecart threat group compromised the British Airways payment transaction portal through a sophisticated Stored Cross-Site Scripting supply-chain attack. By injecting a tiny 22-line JavaScript payload into a trusted third-party script (`modernizr-2.6.2.min.js`), the malicious code operated with full browser privileges. Whenever a traveler entered credit card details, CVVs, names, and billing addresses, the script silently serialized the form inputs and transmitted them via base64 POST requests to an attacker-controlled drop domain (`baways.com`). Over 380,000 customers were compromised, resulting in an unprecedented £20 million ICO regulatory fine. --- ## Code Walkthrough: Vulnerable vs Hardened Implementation ### 1. Vulnerable DOM Sink (Unsafe InnerHTML Injection) ```javascript // INSECURE: Directly interpolating URL query params into the DOM const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search); const userQuery = params.get('q'); // e.g. // The browser parses this string as HTML, triggering the inline onerror payload document.getElementById('search-result').innerHTML = "Results for: " + userQuery; ``` ### 2. Hardened Implementation (Contextual Encoding & DOM APIs) ```typescript // SECURE: Use textContent or DOMPurify with strict typing import DOMPurify from 'dompurify'; export function renderSafeSearchResults(query: string, container: HTMLElement) { // Option A: Safe text node rendering (Zero HTML parsing) container.textContent = `Results for: ${query}`; // Option B: If rich text is required, sanitize through DOMPurify with strict tags const cleanHtml = DOMPurify.sanitize(query, { ALLOWED_TAGS: ['b', 'i', 'em', 'strong'], ALLOWED_ATTR: [] }); // container.innerHTML = cleanHtml; } ``` ![Cybersecurity Sandbox Lab](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1517430816045-df4b7de11d1d?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000) *Figure 2: Inspecting intercepted cookie exfiltration payloads in the WonderCave testing laboratory.* --- ## Point-Based Tiers of Cross-Site Scripting * **Reflected XSS**: The non-persistent variant where the exploit vector arrives in the immediate HTTP request (typically a query parameter) and is reflected back in the immediate HTTP response. Requires phishing social engineering. * **Stored XSS (Persistent)**: The most critical variant where malicious scripts are permanently stored in database records (e.g., user profile bios, comments, product reviews). Every user who visits the page executes the payload automatically. * **DOM-based XSS**: The vulnerability lives completely in client-side JavaScript. The server is never touched; untrusted input from a source (like `location.hash` or `window.name`) flows into an execution sink (like `eval()`, `innerHTML`, or `setTimeout()`). * **Blind XSS**: A subtype of stored XSS where the script executes inside restricted internal administrative portals (such as support ticket dashboards or log viewers) visited only by security staff. --- ## Hardened Defense-in-Depth Checklist 1. **Context-Aware Encoding**: Apply HTML attribute encoding, JavaScript variable encoding, and CSS encoding depending on where input is reflected. 2. **Strict Content Security Policy (CSP)**: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-rAnd0m'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none';` 3. **HttpOnly Cookie Flags**: Ensure session tokens are stamped with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite=Lax` to prevent JavaScript cookie theft. 4. **Use Modern Declarative Frameworks**: React, Vue, and Angular automatically escape variables rendered through JSX expressions (`{userInput}`). --- ## Formal Standards & Academic References * **OWASP Top 10**: [A03:2021 – Injection (Cross-Site Scripting)](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/xss/) * **Common Weakness Enumeration**: [CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html) * **W3C Standard**: Content Security Policy Level 3 Specification * **RFC 6265**: HTTP State Management Mechanism (Cookie Security)

cross-site-request-forgery.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) & SameSite Cookie Architecture
cross-site-request-forgery.subtitle: Exploiting ambient credential transmission, forging state-changing HTTP requests, and implementing cryptographic anti-CSRF defenses.
cross-site-request-forgery.content:
## Executive Threat Profile: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CWE-352) Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF or XSRF) is an attack that forces an authenticated end-user to execute unwanted actions on a web application in which they are currently logged in. By leveraging the browser's default behavior of automatically attaching stored session cookies to cross-origin requests, an attacker can construct malicious links, hidden forms, or image tags on an external site that trigger unauthorized state-changing operations—such as password resets, funds transfers, or email modifications—without the victim's knowledge or consent. ![Browser Security Architecture](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1563986768609-322da13575f3?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000) *Figure 1: Cross-origin browser request routing and ambient session cookie transmission.* --- ## Real-World Breach Case Study: Automated Router DNS Hijacking In a global cybercrime campaign affecting home and small-business broadband gateways, cybercriminals deployed hidden CSRF attack payloads across thousands of high-traffic compromised websites. When an administrator visited one of these infected pages while logged into their router's administrative dashboard (typically hosted on `192.168.1.1`), a hidden auto-submitting form triggered: `POST http://192.168.1.1/setup.cgi?primary_dns=attacker_ip` Because the administrator had an active session cookie stored in their browser, the router accepted the request and altered its primary DNS settings. Millions of users were transparently redirected to fraudulent online banking phishing sites without receiving SSL warning errors. --- ## Code Walkthrough: Vulnerable Form vs Cryptographic Token Guard ### 1. Insecure State-Changing Endpoint (Vulnerable to Ambient Cookie Abuse) ```html
``` ### 2. Hardened Double-Submit Cookie & Synchronizer Token Pattern ```typescript // SECURE: Validating Cryptographically Strong Nonce & SameSite Lax Cookie import crypto from 'crypto'; import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express'; export function csrfProtectionMiddleware(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) { if (['GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS'].includes(req.method)) { return next(); // Safe idempotent methods } const clientToken = req.headers['x-csrf-token'] || req.body._csrf; const sessionToken = req.session?.csrfSecret; if (!clientToken || !sessionToken || clientToken !== sessionToken) { return res.status(403).json({ error: "CSRF verification failed: Invalid origin nonce." }); } next(); } ``` ![Secure Server Infrastructure](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1544197150-b99a580bb7a8?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000) *Figure 2: Verifying cryptographic anti-CSRF token nonces in enterprise proxy headers.* --- ## Point-Based Exploitation Vectors & Browser Mechanics * **Simple GET-Based CSRF**: Exploiting applications that incorrectly accept state-changing operations via GET requests (``). * **Hidden Auto-Submitting POST Forms**: Generating dynamic DOM forms that post multipart or urlencoded payloads across origins. * **CORS Preflight Bypass**: Using standard simple content-types (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `text/plain`, `multipart/form-data`) to avoid triggering browser CORS OPTIONS preflight checks. * **Json CSRF with Flash / Custom Encodings**: Historically abused cross-domain XML policy files; modern mitigations enforce strict Content-Type checking. --- ## Defense-in-Depth Mitigation Checklist 1. **Modern SameSite Cookie Policy**: Set `SameSite=Lax` or `SameSite=Strict` on all session authentication cookies. 2. **Synchronizer Token Pattern (STP)**: Bind a cryptographically random, per-session or per-request token to all mutation forms. 3. **Verify Origin & Referer Headers**: Reject requests where `Origin` does not strictly match the expected host whitelist. 4. **Require Re-Authentication for Sensitive Actions**: Mandate password confirmation or WebAuthn biometrics before executing high-impact state transitions. --- ## Formal Standards & Academic References * **OWASP Top 10**: [A01:2021 – Broken Access Control](https://owasp.org/Top10/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/) * **Common Weakness Enumeration**: [CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/352.html) * **RFC 6749**: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework (State Parameter Anti-CSRF) * **IETF Draft**: Incremental Improvements to SameSite Cookies

xxe-injection.title: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection: Arbitrary File Read & SSRF
xxe-injection.subtitle: Exploiting Document Type Definitions (DTDs), resolving external entities, exfiltrating internal cloud metadata, and disabling DTD parsing.
xxe-injection.content:
## Executive Threat Profile: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection (CWE-611)

XML External Entity (XXE) injection is a critical server-side vulnerability that occurs when an application processes untrusted XML input using a weakly configured or legacy XML parser. The XML specification permits Document Type Definitions (DTDs) to declare custom entities that resolve external URIs. When the parser evaluates external entities, an attacker can coerce the server into reading local system files (such as `/etc/passwd` or cloud credentials), scanning internal network ports, or causing Denial of Service via recursive expansion (the "Billion Laughs" attack).

![Server Architecture and Parser](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1558494949-ef010cbdcc31?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 1: XML DOM parsing engines and external URI resolution boundaries.*

---

## Real-World Breach Case Study: Cloud Metadata Exfiltration via SVG Upload

A major social networking application allowed users to upload custom avatar icons formatted as Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG), an XML-based image format. An attacker uploaded an SVG file containing a malicious external entity targeting AWS EC2 Instance Metadata:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE svg [
  <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/admin-role">
]>
<svg>&xxe;</svg>
```

When the server's background image processor rendered the SVG, it evaluated the `&xxe;` entity, retrieved the temporary AWS IAM secret access keys, and printed them into the converted PNG preview, completely compromising the cloud infrastructure.

---

## Code Walkthrough: Vulnerable XML Parser vs Hardened Configuration

### 1. Insecure Java / Node.js Parser (Default External Resolution Enabled)
```java
// INSECURE: Default XML parser configuration evaluates external entities
DocumentBuilderFactory dbf = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();
// External entity expansion is enabled by default in many legacy frameworks!
DocumentBuilder builder = dbf.newDocumentBuilder();
Document doc = builder.parse(new InputSource(new StringReader(untrustedXml)));
```

### 2. Hardened XML Parser (Completely Disabling DTDs)
```java
// SECURE: Strict feature flags completely disallow inline DTDs and entities
DocumentBuilderFactory dbf = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();
dbf.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true);
dbf.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false);
dbf.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities", false);
dbf.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/nonvalidating/load-external-dtd", false);
dbf.setXIncludeAware(false);
dbf.setExpandEntityReferences(false);
```

![Enterprise Security Command Center](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1526374965328-7f61d4dc18c5?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 2: Simulating blind out-of-band XXE exfiltration via FTP/HTTP listeners.*

---

## Point-Based Exploitation Tiers of XXE

* **In-Band Arbitrary File Read**: The contents of local files (`/etc/passwd` or `C:\Windows\win.ini`) are reflected directly in the application's XML response.
* **Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via XXE**: Forcing the XML parser to make HTTP requests to internal non-routable microservices or cloud metadata services (`169.254.169.254`).
* **Blind Out-of-Band (OOB) XXE**: When the server does not echo XML responses, an external DTD is loaded that embeds the target file's content in the query string of an HTTP or FTP request to an attacker-controlled listener.
* **Billion Laughs / XML Entity Expansion DoS**: Exponential entity recursion that consumes gigabytes of memory within milliseconds, crashing the server process.

---

## Defense-in-Depth Mitigation Checklist

1. **Disable DOCTYPE Declarations Completely**: Ensure `disallow-doctype-decl` is set to true on all XML parser instances.
2. **Disable External Entities & Parameter Entities**: Explicitly toggle parser settings to prevent URI dereferencing.
3. **Prefer Modern Data Formats**: Transition APIs and integrations from XML to strict JSON or Protocol Buffers.
4. **Harden Cloud Metadata Endpoints**: Require IMDSv2 with session tokens on AWS EC2 to block single-packet SSRF from external entity calls.

---

## Formal Standards & Academic References

* **OWASP Top 10**: [A05:2021 – Security Misconfiguration (XXE)](https://owasp.org/www-community/vulnerabilities/XML_External_Entity_(XXE)_Processing)
* **Common Weakness Enumeration**: [CWE-611: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/611.html)
* **NIST SP 800-53**: SI-10 Information Input Validation Controls
* **W3C XML Recommendation**: Extensible Markup Language (XML) 1.0 DTD Entity Rules

web-cache-deception.title: Web Cache Deception (WCD) & Cache Poisoning Defense
web-cache-deception.subtitle: Manipulating Content Delivery Networks (CDNs), path delimiter discrepancies, and harvesting cached private user data.
web-cache-deception.content:
## Executive Threat Profile: Web Cache Deception (CWE-524)

Web Cache Deception (WCD) occurs when an application server and an intermediary caching proxy (such as Cloudflare, Akamai, Varnish, or Fastly) interpret URL path delimiters, extensions, or file types inconsistently. By appending a static file extension (like `/test.css` or `/avatar.png`) to a private, dynamic endpoint (such as `/account/settings`), an attacker tricks the CDN into caching private user account records as if they were public static assets, allowing the attacker to harvest the cached confidential data at will.

![CDN and Proxy Infrastructure](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1451187580459-43490279c0fa?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 1: Path normalization and discrepancy analysis between CDN edge proxies and backend microservices.*

---

## Real-World Breach Case Study: PayPal Web Cache Deception Discovery

In 2017, security researcher Omer Gil discovered a critical Web Cache Deception flaw in PayPal's user profile infrastructure. By sending a logged-in user a link formatted like:
`https://paypal.com/myaccount/home/customer.css`

The browser requested the URL with the victim's session cookies. The backend application discarded the suffix `/customer.css` and returned the victim's personal profile data, credit card last-four digits, and transaction history. Concurrently, the CDN observed the `.css` file extension, classified the HTTP 200 response as a public static stylesheet, and cached it in edge memory for 5 hours. Gil then accessed the exact same URL without authentication and retrieved the victim's complete personal profile.

---

## Code Comparison: Vulnerable Proxy Rules vs Hardened Cache Control

### 1. Insecure Caching Rule (Matching Extension Without Content-Type Validation)
```nginx
# INSECURE: Caches purely based on request URL regex regardless of headers
location ~* \.(css|js|png|jpg|jpeg|gif|ico|svg)$ {
    proxy_pass http://backend_upstream;
    proxy_cache my_cdn_cache;
    proxy_cache_valid 200 60m;
    # FLAW: Fails to inspect backend 'Cache-Control' headers!
}
```

### 2. Hardened Architecture (Strict Cache-Control & Path Normalization)
```typescript
// SECURE: Backend always emits explicit anti-caching headers on dynamic data
import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';

export function enforcePrivateCachePolicy(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
  // Prevent any intermediary proxy from storing dynamic state
  res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private');
  res.setHeader('Pragma', 'no-cache');
  res.setHeader('Expires', '0');
  res.setHeader('X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff');
  
  next();
}
```

![Cloudflare Edge Network](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1558494949-ef010cbdcc31?auto=format&fit=crop&q=80&w=1000)
*Figure 2: Verifying Cache-Control headers and edge hit/miss status in Cloudflare Workers debugging.*

---

## Point-Based Mechanics of Web Cache Deception

* **Path Mapping Discrepancy**: Occurs when frameworks (like Spring MVC or Rails) use flexible route matching that ignores trailing delimiters or path suffixes.
* **Delimiter Inconsistency**: Characters such as semicolons (`;`), hashes (`#`), questions marks (`?`), or encoded forward slashes (`%2F`) are parsed differently by edge servers and upstream origin servers.
* **Cache Key Poisoning vs Cache Deception**:
  * *Deception*: The victim visits the malicious URL and gets their private data saved in the cache. The attacker then downloads it.
  * *Poisoning*: The attacker sends a crafted payload that gets cached and subsequently served to all legitimate users (e.g. stored XSS via HTTP Host headers).

---

## Hardened Defense-in-Depth Checklist

1. **Emit Explicit Cache-Control Directives**: Dynamic endpoints must emit `Cache-Control: private, no-store` to override proxy assumptions.
2. **Align Path Delimiter Rules**: Ensure backend web servers and CDN edge proxies strictly reject unrecognized path suffixes with 404 responses.
3. **Verify Response Content-Type Before Caching**: Proxies must confirm that an asset claiming to be `.css` returns `Content-Type: text/css` before saving to cache.
4. **Isolate Static and Dynamic Hostnames**: Host public assets exclusively on separate subdomains (e.g., `static.wondercave.com`) completely isolated from authenticated user sessions.

---

## Formal Standards & Academic References

* **Common Weakness Enumeration**: [CWE-524: Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/524.html)
* **RFC 9111**: HTTP Caching Architecture Specification
* **PortSwigger Research**: Web Cache Deception & Cache Poisoning Masterclass
* **OWASP**: Testing for Web Cache Deception Guidelines

manufacturing.title: Manufacturing & Industrial Security
manufacturing.subtitle: Defending Operational Technology (OT), SCADA, and connected supply chains.
manufacturing.content:
## Industrial Cybersecurity Blueprint

As manufacturing facilities converge Operational Technology (OT) and Information Technology (IT), industrial control systems (ICS) and SCADA networks become prime targets for ransomware and espionage.

### Key Attack Vectors in Manufacturing

* **Supply Chain Interdependence**: Insecure vendor remote-access tunnels exposing assembly telemetry.
* **Air-Gap Bridges**: Accidental or unauthorized IoT bridges transmitting untrusted traffic into isolated production zones.
* **Legacy Firmware**: Unpatched embedded controllers vulnerable to remote command injection.

### WonderCave Defensive Strategy

1. Enforce strict micro-segmentation between corporate ERP and factory-floor controllers.
2. Deploy non-intrusive passive vulnerability monitors that assess SCADA interfaces without interrupting continuous production.
3. Integrate hardware token multifactor authentication for all engineering maintenance terminals.

retail.title: Retail & E-Commerce Security
retail.subtitle: Protecting digital storefronts, checkout APIs, and cardholder data.
retail.content:
## Defending Global Digital Commerce

Modern e-commerce platforms handle millions of concurrent financial transactions daily. Attackers target checkout funnels, third-party marketing tags, and inventory databases through Magecart-style skimmers and account takeover bots.

### Threat Landscape

* **Digital Skimming (Magecart)**: Injected malicious scripts intercepting payment card data directly in client browsers.
* **Inventory Hoarding & Botting**: Automated scrapers hoarding sale inventory and overwhelming database backends.
* **Credential Stuffing**: High-frequency authentication attempts leveraging leaked credential lists.

### Architecture Countermeasures

* **Strict Content Security Policy (CSP)**: Disallow unauthorized external script execution and enforce Subresource Integrity (SRI) on all third-party tag managers.
* **Behavioral Bot Management**: Transparent challenge mechanisms that verify human intent without degrading checkout conversion rates.
* **PCI-DSS Level 1 Compliance**: Continuous automated scanning of all payment endpoints and cryptographic key rotation.

healthcare.title: Healthcare Information Security
healthcare.subtitle: HIPAA-compliant shielding for electronic health records (EHR) and telemetry.
healthcare.content:
## Securing Patient Care & Telehealth Systems

Healthcare organizations operate in high-consequence environments where data confidentiality directly impacts patient safety and trust. Modern hospital networks link diagnostic equipment, patient portals, and insurance claim APIs.

### Core Healthcare Vulnerabilities

* **Electronic Health Record (EHR) Exposure**: Unauthenticated GraphQL or REST endpoints leaking Protected Health Information (PHI).
* **Medical IoT (IoMT)**: Connected infusion pumps and vital monitors lacking cryptographic firmware validation.
* **Ransomware Disruption**: Targeted extortion attacks seeking to cripple acute care facilities.

### Protective Framework

* **Zero-Trust Network Architecture**: Continuous authentication and least-privilege scoping across all medical workstations.
* **Automated HIPAA Audit Logging**: Immutable cryptographic audit trails tracking every read, query, and modification of patient records.
* **Proactive Web Scanner Assessments**: Scheduled non-disruptive scans of hospital scheduling portals and telehealth webRTC servers.

cors.title: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Misconfigurations
cors.subtitle: Exploiting permissive CORS headers to extract sensitive user data.
cors.content:
## Vulnerability Mechanics

CORS allows servers to specify which external origins are allowed to read responses. Insecure server configurations often trust arbitrary `Origin` request headers or incorrectly reflect origins containing `null`:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
```

### Exploitation Technique

An attacker hosts a malicious web page that makes an authenticated `fetch()` call to the vulnerable API. Because `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is true, the victim's session cookies are transmitted and the attacker reads the private response body.

### Remediation

* Never reflect the `Origin` header blindly in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
* Maintain an explicit whitelist of trusted origins.
* Avoid setting `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` when wildcard origins (`*`) or dynamically generated origins are used.

command-injection.title: OS Command Injection
command-injection.subtitle: Executing arbitrary operating system commands on the server.
command-injection.content:
## Overview & Impact

Command injection occurs when an application passes user-supplied data into a system shell (e.g. `system()`, `exec()`, `execSync`) without proper validation or parameter separation.

```bash
# Insecure server script
ping -c 1 $USER_INPUT
# Attacker payload: 127.0.0.1; cat /etc/passwd
```

### Consequences

Successful execution gives the attacker full control of the host operating system under the privileges of the web process, enabling lateral network movement and data exfiltration.

### Prevention

* Avoid executing shell commands directly.
* If system operations are necessary, use built-in language APIs rather than shell wrappers.
* When commands must be executed, use parameterized command execution arrays without invoking `/bin/sh` or `cmd.exe`.

access-control.title: Broken Access Control
access-control.subtitle: Bypassing authorization boundaries and privilege escalation.
access-control.content:
## Overview

Broken access control occurs when users can execute actions or view data outside of their intended permissions. It ranks as the #1 threat in the OWASP Top 10.

### Common Varieties

* **Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR)**: Accessing `/api/documents/104` when the user only owns document 102.
* **Vertical Privilege Escalation**: Regular users accessing administrative endpoints like `/api/admin/delete-user`.
* **CORS and Token Tampering**: Altering claims in unsigned JWT tokens to impersonate superusers.

### Defensive Principles

* Enforce authorization centrally on the server for every endpoint.
* Deny access by default.
* Implement record-level ownership checks before executing database queries.

jwt-attacks.title: JSON Web Token (JWT) Attacks
jwt-attacks.subtitle: Cracking, tampering, and bypassing token-based authentication.
jwt-attacks.content:
## Threat Overview

JSON Web Tokens are widely used for stateless authentication. Vulnerabilities typically stem from faulty signature verification, insecure key distribution, or algorithm confusion.

### Critical Flaws

* **Algorithm Switching (None Algorithm)**: Changing the header `"alg": "none"` to bypass signature checks completely.
* **Weak HMAC Secrets**: Brute-forcing predictable symmetric signing keys using hashcat.
* **Key Injection (JWK Header)**: Embedding an attacker-controlled public key directly in the token header.

### Best Practices

* Always enforce strong cryptographic algorithms (e.g. RS256 or ES256) on the server.
* Reject tokens with `"alg": "none"` explicitly.
* Verify expiration timestamps (`exp`) and audience claims (`aud`).

race-conditions.title: Race Conditions & Concurrency Flaws
race-conditions.subtitle: Exploiting multi-threaded request processing windows.
race-conditions.content:
## Mechanics of Race Conditions

Race conditions occur when web applications execute multiple operations concurrently without adequate synchronization locks. This creates a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability.

### Example Exploits

* **Double-Spending**: Submitting identical checkout requests simultaneously to apply a single coupon multiple times.
* **Rate Limit Bypass**: Flooding an authentication endpoint with concurrent password guesses before the failure counter increments.

### Remediation

* Use database transactions with appropriate isolation levels (e.g. Serializable).
* Implement distributed locks (e.g. Redis Redlock) around critical state transitions.
* Use atomic SQL update operations (e.g. `UPDATE balances SET amount = amount - ? WHERE amount >= ?`).
